ety.text: Unclear. Possibly related to cys (“to goad”). Alternatively, related to Greek τσίτα (tsíta, “pin, hairpin”). To be noted is the existence of sahitë (“knitting needle”), from Greek σαΐτα (saḯta, “arrow”), ultimately from Latin sagitta, which might be the common source.

From Proto-Albanian *spesla, metathesized form of *spelsa, from Proto-Indo-European *pels- (“rock, boulder”), variant of *spel- (“to cleave, break”). Compare Latin hydronym Pelso, Latin Palatium, Pashto پرښه (parša, “rock, rocky ledge”), Ancient Greek πέλλα (pélla, “stone”), German Felsen (“boulder, cliff”). Mostly dialectal, used in Gheg Albanian.
Possibly from Vulgar Latin form *carabriōnem, from Latin crābrōnem.
From hundë (“nose”) + shtypur (“pressed”)
Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian ìnćūn /ѝнћӯн. Doublet of açugë and ançua.

Variant of dialectal ap, from Proto-Albanian *apa, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁op-eio/e-, from *h₁ep- (“to take”). The verb is suppletive with past dhashë and participle dhënë from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃-.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin capreolus ("roe deer, roe buck").

ety.text: Back-formation from variant krife (plurale tantum), from Proto-Albanian *kripsijā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱripes- (“headhair”) (compare Latin crinis (“mane”)). More at krip.
Perhaps akin to kucur (“log stump”) or shkurre (“shrub”).

s.g: Eucharist (the holy bread and wine used in the cerimony)

ety.text: From kungoj (“to communicate”) + -atë.

From Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright, to shine; to see”). Cognate to Ancient Greek λευκός (leukós, “gleaming, white”), Latin lux (“light”), Welsh llug (“radiance”), Lithuanian laũkas (“pale”), Old Norse ljos (“light”).
Probably a learned borrowing from Latin māchina, ultimately from Doric Greek μᾱχᾰνᾱ́ (mākhănā́). Doublet of mokër.

s.g: Myzeqe (a geographic region and plain of the Western Lowlands, Albania)

ety.text: A development of medieval Albanian Muzaka, likely through Italian Musacchia, though the ultimate origin of the name is unclear: * A local Albanian derivation would be from Albanian mëzak (“young calf”); * Johan Georg Von Hahn derived it from Illyrian; * Gjon Muzaka from Ancient Greek Μολοσσοί (Molossoí); * Zef Jubani from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ).

Widely considered to be a borrowing through Vulgar Latin, from Latin hospitium, via a metathesis from hospitium to hostipium; compare Ancient Greek ὁσπίτιον (hospítion) (modern Greek σπίτι (spíti)). The contracted form shpi is due to syllable reduction from shtëpi. However, there are still phonetic difficulties.
